props.title: How does observation instigate scientific investigation?

props.statement: carry out a practical investigation to record both quantitative and qualitative data from observations
discuss and evaluate the characteristics of observations made compared to inferences drawn in respect of the practical investigation
research how observation has instigated experimentation to investigate cause and effect in historical examples

assess ways in which Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples use observation to develop an understanding of Country and Place in order to create innovative ways of managing the natural environment

props.title: What are the benefits and drawbacks of qualitative and quantitative observations?

props.statement: carry out a practical activity to qualitatively and quantitatively describe
analyse the quantitative data from the following information sources
evaluate the differences between qualitative and quantitative observations and data and where these are used

props.title: How does primary data provide evidence for further investigation?

props.statement: use data gathered to plan a practical investigation
develop a method to collect primary data for a practical investigation
evaluate how observation is limited by the observational tools available

props.title: How does the collection and presentation of primary data affect the outcome of a scientific investigation?

props.statement: carry out the planned practical investigation, above, to collect primary data
apply conventions for collecting and recording observations to qualitatively and quantitatively analyse the primary data
compare the usefulness of observations recorded in the initial practical activity with the primary data gathered in this planned practical investigation

props.title: How do conclusions drawn from the interpretation of primary data promote further scientific investigation?

props.statement: draw conclusions from the analysis of the primary data collected in the practical investigation
evaluate the process of drawing conclusions from the primary data collected
assess the findings of the scientific investigation in relation to the findings of other related investigations
assess the need to make further observations by gathering data about other phenomena arising from the practical investigation

props.title: What inferences can be drawn from observations?

props.statement: investigate the practices of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples that relate to observations and inferences
conduct a collaborative practical investigation and collect a range of qualitative and quantitative primary data
make inferences and conclusions derived from the primary data collected in this collaborative practical investigation

props.title: How is secondary-sourced data used in practical investigations?

props.statement: collect qualitative and quantitative secondary-sourced data to validate the inferences and conclusions drawn from the practical investigation
discuss how secondary-sourced data adds to the inferences and conclusions drawn from primary data
evaluate the usefulness of considering secondary-sourced research before undertaking an investigation to collect primary data

props.title: How does humans' ability to recognise patterns affect the way they interpret data?

props.statement: describe patterns that have been observed over time throughout the Universe and in nature
interpret data in order to propose a hypothesis based on an irregular pattern observed over time in the Universe and in nature
examine the human tendency to observe patterns and misinterpret information
discuss how the tendency to recognise patterns, even when they may not exist, can lead to misinterpretation of data
discuss the role and significance of outliers in data

props.title: How can hypotheses and assumptions be tested?

props.statement: gather secondary-sourced data describing historical instances of long-standing assumptions that have been updated by scientific investigation
propose an inquiry question, construct a hypothesis and conduct an investigation that tests a common assumption
use appropriate representations to analyse the data

props.title: What generalisations and assumptions are made from observed data?

props.statement: make generalisations to describe any trends found in the data
draw conclusion based on generalisations

props.title: What role do peers play in scientific investigation?

props.statement: assess the input that collaborative teams and alternative perspectives have had on the development of hypotheses and research questions
assess the scientific community's current understanding of scientific mysteries and outline why this understanding remains incomplete
evaluate biases that may have affected the scientific thinking of European settlers about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' ecological understanding and knowledge

props.title: What is a scientific model?

props.statement: examine the types of models that may be used in science

props.title: What makes scientific models useful?

props.statement: examine the use of scientific models
outline how models have been used to illustrate, simplify and represent scientific concepts and processes
explain how scientific models are used to make predictions that are difficult to analyse in the real world
assess the effectiveness of models at facilitating the understanding of scientific processes, structures and mathematical relationships
evaluate how scientific models draw on a growing body of data from a wide range of disciplines and technologies to refine predictions and test new hypotheses

props.title: When should a particular model be used?

props.statement: explain why new evidence can challenge the use of existing scientific models and may result in those models being contested and refined or replaced
compare the limitations of simple and complex scientific models

props.title: How can a model be constructed to simplify understanding of a scientific concept?

props.statement: investigate a scientific concept or process that can be represented using a model

props.title: What are the differences and similarities between scientific theories and laws?

props.statement: collect primary data to investigate the law of conservation of mass
collect secondary-sourced data to investigate the theory of plate tectonics
compare the characteristics of theories and laws

props.title: What leads to a theory being developed?

props.statement: gather secondary-sourced data to investigate the supporting evidence and development of theories
gather secondary-sourced data to investigate how aspects of a theory can be disproved through the collection of evidence

props.title: What leads to the acceptance of a scientific law?

props.statement: gather secondary-sourced data to investigate and assess the evidence that supports scientific laws
design and collect primary data to show that results can be predicted by laws

props.title: How are theories and laws used in science?

props.statement: investigate how the law of conservation of energy is applied in different science disciplines
demonstrate, using evidence and examples, how diverse phenomena have been unified into specific theories

gather secondary-sourced data to investigate how scientific investigations of nuclear reactions and decay changed the way in which the law of conservation of mass and law of conservation of energy are interpreted

props.title: What initiates an investigation?

props.statement: research the factors that led scientists to investigate the following
propose a reason for the scientists undertaking their investigations above by examining the type of data or information that they sought
determine the hypotheses that were tested in each of the scientific investigations above
describe where deviations from the traditional and linear models of scientific methodology were necessary in order to test each hypothesis

props.title: What type of methodology best suits a scientific investigation?

props.statement: using examples, evaluate the objectives and data collected in an investigation by a recognised scientist or team of scientists
evaluate the methodology of the scientific investigations above
develop a method most appropriate to test a hypothesis following observation
justify the type of methodology used to test the hypothesis

props.title: How is the integrity of a scientific investigation judged?

props.statement: evaluate the design of the student investigation
conduct the planned investigation and collect, record and analyse primary data
draw a conclusion or conclusions, and suggest further investigation or research
evaluate the validity of the investigation
props.definition: An experiment is valid if its method is appropriate and directly tests the intended hypothesis. Core components include controlling variables, having a single independent variable, and appropriate measurement of the dependent variable.
props.hsc_example: (2021 Q22b - GMO Mice): An experiment tested if genetically modified mice on a high-fat diet gained more weight. To be valid, it required four groups to isolate the effects of the gene and the diet, including a control group (normal mice, normal diet) and a hypothesis test group (GMO mice, high-fat diet).

props.statement: evaluate the reliability of the investigation
props.definition: An experiment is reliable if the results are consistent and repeatable. This is achieved through repetition (at least 3 trials) and using a sufficiently large sample size.
props.hsc_example: (2020 Q25a - Self-Injection): A researcher injected herself with a bacterium to see if it caused a disease. This experiment is unreliable because the sample size is only one, making it impossible to know if the result is consistent or a one-off personal reaction.

props.title: What is the structure of an investigative report?

props.statement: review a published and peer-reviewed scientific report to determine the conventions of writing a report on a practical investigation
props.definition: A formal scientific report follows a clear structure (Aim, Hypothesis, Method, Results, Discussion, Conclusion). The language must be objective, in the third person, and use precise scientific terminology.
props.hsc_example: (2023 Q30 - Student Report): A student's report was criticised for using informal headings like 'My prediction is' instead of 'Hypothesis' and for describing results with colloquial language ('spurt height') instead of quantitative data in a table.

props.statement: use a sample of a published and peer-reviewed secondary source to identify the purpose, language style, presentation and structure of the report
compare and contrast the structures and functions of a scientific investigation and its written report
prepare a report on the student investigation that was carried out

props.note: Evaluating the validity of an investigation is a key component of evaluating the overall process.
Evaluating the reliability of an investigation is a key component of evaluating the overall process.
Understanding the conventions of scientific reports is essential for communicating scientific understanding.

props.title: How does technology enhance and/or limit scientific investigation?

props.statement: design a practical investigation that uses available technologies to measure both the independent and dependent variables that produce quantitative data
conduct the practical investigation to obtain relevant data and evaluate the limitations of the technologies used
investigate the range of measuring devices used in the practical investigation and assess the likelihood of random and systematic errors and the devices' degree of accuracy
using specific examples, compare the accuracy of analogue and digital technologies in making observations
assess the safety of technologies selected for the practical investigation by using chemical safety data and Work Health and Safety guidelines

props.title: How have developments in technology led to advances in scientific theories and laws that, in turn, drive the need for further developments in technology?

props.statement: using examples, assess the impact that developments in technologies have had on the accumulation of evidence for scientific theories, laws and models
props.definition: Science and technology have a feedback loop. New technology enables new scientific understanding, which in turn enables the development of even newer technology.
props.hsc_example: (2024 Q36 - DNA & GMOs): X-ray crystallography (technology) was essential for Franklin to produce Photo 51. This image (science) allowed Watson and Crick to develop the double helix model of DNA. This new understanding enabled the development of recombinant DNA technology to create GMOs (new technology).

props.statement: using examples, assess the impact that developments in scientific theories, laws and models have had on the development of new technologies
investigate scientists' increasing awareness of the value of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' knowledge and understanding of the medicinal and material uses of plants

props.note: Understanding the feedback loop between science and technology is key to describing how science drives technological development.

props.title: How can a claim be tested?

props.statement: plan and conduct an investigation based on testing a claim
using examples, evaluate the impact that sample selection and sample sizes can have on the results of an investigation
compare emotive advertising with evidence-based claims

props.title: What factors can affect the way data can be interpreted, analysed and understood?

props.statement: using examples, justify the use of placebos, double-blind trials and control groups in order to draw valid conclusions
evaluate the impact of societal and economic influences on the collection and interpretation of data

props.title: What type of evidence is needed to draw valid conclusions?

props.statement: evaluate how evidence of a correlation can be misinterpreted as causation
props.definition: Correlation is a relationship where two variables change together, but it does not imply one causes the other. Causation is where a change in one variable directly causes a change in another. Mistaking correlation for causation is a common logical fallacy.
props.hsc_example: (2019 Q25c - Whales & CO₂): A graph showed that as whale sightings increased, atmospheric CO₂ also increased. A student incorrectly infers that the whales cause the increase in CO₂. This is a correlation, not causation, as a third factor (e.g., global economic growth) could be responsible for both trends.

props.title: How does the reporting of science influence the general public's understanding of the subject?

props.statement: examine a contemporary scientific debate and how it is portrayed in the mainstream media
evaluate the use and interpretation of the terms 'theory', 'hypothesis', 'belief' and 'law' in relation to media reporting of scientific developments
compare the difference in reporting between a peer-reviewed journal article and a scientific article published in popular media
analyse how conflicts of interest can result in scientific evidence being suppressed, misinterpreted or misrepresented
describe the halo effect and, using examples, explain how the influence of positive perceptions can result in the rejection of valid alternative perspectives
using examples, analyse a pseudo-scientific claim and how scientific language and processes can be manipulated to sway public opinion
props.definition: Pseudoscience is a claim, belief, or practice presented as scientific, but which does not adhere to the scientific method. It often uses scientific-sounding language to mislead.
props.hsc_example: (2020 Q27a - Astrology): Astrologists use scientific-sounding terms like 'retrograde motion' to give their claims an appearance of scientific legitimacy, misleading the public into believing astrology is based on scientific evidence when it is not testable or falsifiable.

props.title: Can the scientific community and process of peer review find 'the truth'?

props.statement: conduct an investigation using secondary sources to research a scientist who has falsified their scientific experimental results
analyse the scientific debate surrounding 'publication' and discuss the implications of scientists' need to 'publish or perish'
evaluate the increasing volume of scientific papers being published and assess the feasibility of science to effectively manage, review, replicate and validate investigations
analyse the benefits of peer review in relation to the advancement of science
props.definition: Peer review is the evaluation of scientific work by other experts in the same field to ensure its quality and validity before it is published. It acts as a critical quality control filter.
props.hsc_example: (2019 Q29b - Marshall & Warren): Marshall and Warren's paper on H. pylori causing ulcers was peer-reviewed before publication. This process ensured their revolutionary idea was scrutinised for validity and methodological rigour, which helped it gain acceptance and advance medicine.

props.statement: discuss the impact of fake science journals on the public perception of science

props.note: Understanding the difference between correlation and causation is fundamental to using evidence-based analysis to support or refute a hypothesis.
Analysing pseudo-scientific claims is a key problem-solving skill.
Understanding peer review is key to analysing and evaluating secondary data.

props.title: How do science-related events affect society's view of science?

props.statement: investigate case studies of past events to consider how they have affected the public image of science

props.title: Why is scientific research regulated?

props.statement: investigate the need for the regulation of scientific research
investigate and assess ethical issues surrounding current scientific research
props.definition: Ethical research is governed by core principles (NHMRC): Informed Consent (participants are briefed on risks), Beneficence (maximise benefits, minimise harm), and Justice (fair selection of participants).
props.hsc_example: (2020 Q25b - Ethics Committee): For a researcher who self-injected a bacterium, an ethics committee would likely require prior investigation on animal models to decrease the risk of human harm and would enforce strict animal welfare protocols.

props.statement: investigate a range of international scientific codes of conduct in regard to scientific research and practice
evaluate the effectiveness of international regulation in scientific research and practice

props.title: How do economic, social and political influences affect scientific research?

props.statement: evaluate the costs involved in space exploration compared to investments in social issues
evaluate how scientific research aids economic development and human progress
evaluate the impacts of scientific research, devices and applications on world health and human wellbeing
using examples, analyse the impacts that governments and large corporations have on scientific research
props.definition: Economic and political forces significantly influence science. A conflict of interest occurs when a researcher's private interests (e.g., financial ties to a company) could improperly influence their professional judgment.
props.hsc_example: (2022 Q33b - Corporate Funding & 2020 Q32c - Climate Change): Increased corporate funding for science can create pressure for results favourable to the funder's products. An astrophysicist funded by oil companies claiming water vapour is the main cause of climate change is a major conflict of interest, as the fossil fuel industry has a financial stake in downplaying CO₂'s role.

props.statement: evaluate how personal, cultural and socioeconomic perspectives can influence the direction of scientific research
props.definition: Social and political factors influence science. Scientific evidence can be used to inform political decisions and shape public opinion.
props.hsc_example: (2019 Q30b - Franklin River Dam): Scientists provided evidence on the negative environmental impacts of a proposed dam. This evidence was used by activists (social factor) and ultimately influenced a High Court decision to stop the dam (political outcome), demonstrating the interplay between science and society.

props.note: Assessing ethical issues is a core component of evaluating ethical influences on science.
Analysing the impact of corporations and governments is a core component of evaluating economic and political influences on science.
Evaluating socioeconomic perspectives is a core component of evaluating social influences on science.
